# 

# **1\. Introduction**

ILAQA is a mobile running game. It turns real city streets into territory you can claim. As you run, the app tracks your path with Google Maps. Complete a full loop around a block or park, and that area becomes yours. We built this with privacy in mind. It gives regular runs a fun, game-like twist without exposing your live location. You just need your phone with you to play.

# **2\. Objective**

We want to build a GPS running app that lets people claim real-world land by running around it. We are adding energy rules, levels, leaderboards, and timed races. We use React Native for the front end, ASP.NET Core for the back end, and Google Maps to draw the board.

# **3\. Problem Description**

Most fitness apps track speed and distance. That gets boring fast. Games like Pokémon GO get people moving, but they do not require real physical effort. ILAQA fills that gap. It combines accurate run tracking with a fun map game. Privacy is usually a problem in location apps, so we hide exact runner locations from the public. This gives runners in Karachi a clear reason to keep active while staying safe.

# **4\. Target Industry**

This sits mainly in Health & Fitness and Sports Tech. It also touches mobile gaming and local community events, starting with university runners in Karachi.

**5\. Methodology**  
We build this step by step in two-week work cycles across FYP-I and FYP-II. Here is how the tech works:

* **Tracking & Maps:** We use the Google Maps SDK inside React Native to show paths and territories on screen.  
* **Data Handling:** ASP.NET Core runs the server side and takes in raw GPS data safely.  
* **Map Rules:** We clean up noisy GPS points and snap them to actual roads using Google Roads API. NetTopologySuite then checks three things: did you finish near your start, did you enclose a real area (simple back-and-forth runs do not count), and did your path avoid crossing itself? If all three pass, PostGIS saves the territory.  
* **Privacy Design:** The server handles location processing. Public users and guests only see leaderboard scores and overall territory shapes, never live runner locations.

# **6\. Project Scope**

**Cross-Platform Mobile App:** A fully functioning iOS and Android application built with React Native and Expo. This includes the core user interfaces for profiles, live leaderboards, and basic competition brackets.  
**Backend & Server API:** An ASP.NET Core web platform to manage the data. We aren't just testing this on local developer machines—the API is validated using data from real-world runs in Karachi to make sure the tracking actually holds up in the field.  
**Active Push Alerts:** Custom notifications to keep users engaged and informed when competition standings change.  
**Anti-Cheating System:** A security layer built specifically to avoid users spoofing their GPS coordinates, logging impossible run paces, or using emulators to manipulate the leaderboards. If the data isn't authentic, it gets flagged.

**7\. Feasibility Study**  
We can finish this project within the one-year timeline if we manage these risks and resources well:

## **7.1 Risks Involved:**

**Risk:** Constant location tracking drains phone batteries fast.

* *Fix:* Send GPS updates in batches through React Native instead of streaming every single second.

**Risk:** Google Maps API usage costs can rise quickly.

* *Fix:* Track API requests carefully, store map data locally when possible, and keep keys locked to test setups to stay inside free limits.

**Risk:** People might cheat using bikes or slow cars to claim land without running.

*Fix:* We use two checks. First, we throw out runs that go faster than humanly possible. Second, we compare GPS distance against actual steps using Expo Sensors. Suspicious accounts get flagged.

## **API Cost & Resource Management:**

During live testing in Karachi, Google Maps SDK and Google Roads API usage is strictly optimized to stay within free tier limits. Location points are batched and cached locally using Expo SQLite before sending requests to the Google Roads API for snap-to-road processing. Additionally, API keys are restricted to test environments and rate-limited to avoid unexpected costs during high-frequency GPS recording.

**Risk:** Continuous GPS tracking in mobile apps can drain batteries quickly and get killed by mobile OS background restrictions.

*Fix:* Utilize batch updates and distance-filtered location tracking (e.g., recording a point only after moving 5–10 meters) rather than continuous time-interval streaming.

## **7.2 Resource Requirement:**

* Development laptops that can run Android and iOS simulators alongside Expo Go.  
* A cloud-hosted PostgreSQL database with PostGIS enabled.  
* A web server setup that runs ASP.NET Core (.NET 8+).  
* A Google Cloud account to access the Maps SDK and Roads API.  
* Outdoor running routes in Karachi for live testing.

* Figma for design, and GitHub Projects for task tracking. 

 **7.3 Security Considerations**

> * **Password storage:** ASP.NET Core Identity handles user logins. It salts and hashes passwords using PBKDF2. We never save plain text passwords.  
> * **Login tokens:** JWT access tokens expire quickly (like in 15 minutes). The app refreshes them silently in the background using secure refresh tokens stored in Expo SecureStore. You will not get logged out mid-run.  
> * **Access checks:** When you edit a territory or run, the server double-checks that you own it. Changing numbers in a web link will not give you someone else's data.  
> * **Secure traffic:** All app data travels over HTTPS/TLS. The server drops unsecured connections.  
> * **Database protection:** Entity Framework Core uses safe parameter queries automatically, stopping SQL attacks.  
> * **Input checks:** We validate incoming data models before saving anything to the database, blocking bad or oversized requests early.  
> * **Rate limits:** We limit login attempts to stop password guessing. GPS uploads have a generous limit (20 requests a minute per user) so normal runs go through easily while spam gets blocked.  
> * **Traffic shields:** Cloudflare or Railway filters large web attacks before they reach our API servers.  
> * **Conflict locks:** If two runners claim the exact same territory at the same time, the server locks that row and handles claims one by one. This prevents glitchy double ownership.  
> * **API locks:** CORS rules lock the API so random websites cannot call our servers directly.  
> * **Location privacy:** Raw, live GPS coordinates stay internal. The app only shows overall territory shapes and leaderboard totals publicly.

# **8\. Solution Application Areas**

Running apps lose users quickly. ILAQA fixes this by turning runs into friendly turf wars. It gives Karachi runners a real reason to stick with their workout routines. Local clubs and university groups can run city-wide races without buying extra gear. Down the road, this setup leaves room for local brand partnerships once the core app proves itself with active runners.

# **9\. Tools/Technology**

Here is a quick look at our tech tools.  
It matches our core stack (React Native, ASP.NET Core, and Google Maps). Keeping the descriptions simple gives us flexibility if we tweak smaller helper libraries later.  
We chose tools that speed up cross-platform development while keeping map calculations fast. These choices form our core setup, though small utility tools may evolve during development.  
**Mobile Application (Frontend)**

* **React Native (Expo):** Lets us build for iOS and Android using one shared code base. Expo makes testing simple on physical phones.  
* **Google Maps SDK (react-native-maps):** Renders live runner locations, city streets, and territory shapes clearly.  
* **Expo Location:** Gathers GPS coordinates efficiently in the background without killing battery life.  
* **Standard React Setup:** Uses standard tools for app state, secure token storage, and web requests (like Fetch/Axios) to keep the app small.

**Backend API**

* **ASP.NET Core (C\#):** A dependable framework that handles server logic, user logins, and spatial checks.  
* **Entity Framework (EF) Core:** Connects the server code to the database safely and manages schema updates.  
* **NetTopologySuite:** A C\# spatial library that checks if a path forms a closed loop before saving it.  
* **JWT Logins:** Keeps user sessions secure while separating full accounts from guest users.

**Database & Spatial Storage**

* **PostgreSQL:** A reliable database for user accounts, run history, and rankings.  
* **PostGIS:** Handles spatial data. Instead of saving raw text coordinates, it stores territories as clean geometric shapes.  
* **Spatial Indexing:** Indexes (like GiST) speed up map searches, loading nearby blocks quickly without searching the full database.

**Anti-Cheat & Sensors**

* **Expo Sensors (Pedometer):** Checks step counts against GPS distance to catch people driving or riding bikes.  
* **Expo Location Alerts:** Triggers local phone notifications when you enter a contested territory, saving server calls.

**Algorithms Used**

* **GPS filtering —** Removes GPS points that are clearly wrong (sudden jumps, duplicates, or points too close together).  
* **Road snapping —** Moves each GPS point to the closest point on a real road or path (via the Google Roads API).  
* **Closed-loop check —** Measures the distance between the run's start point and end point, to check the runner came back to where they started.  
* **Enclosed-area check —** Calculates the area enclosed by the route, to make sure it is a real loop and not a straight there-and-back run.  
* **Self-intersection check —** Checks whether the route crosses itself in a way that would break the shape.  
* **Polygon generation —** Turns the validated route into a polygon shape and works out its area (using PostGIS).  
* **Leaderboard ranking —** Keeps the leaderboard sorted and quick to read, even as scores keep changing.  
* **Scheduled background jobs — No login for** 3 days may cause losing your territory.

**Hosting**

* **Vercel —** Hosts the website.  
* **Azure —** Hosts the backend server.  
* **Supabase —** Hosts the PostgreSQL \+ PostGIS database.  
* **Expo EAS Build —** Builds the mobile app into installable iOS/Android files.  
* **Cloudinary —** Stores profile pictures and other images, instead of storing them in the database.  
* **Sentry —** Tracks errors in the app so bugs can be found and fixed quickly.

**11\. Milestones**  
Here are the main milestones for our year-long project, split across FYP-I and FYP-II.

**System Architecture & Data Flow Explanation:**  
The system architecture follows a structured data flow between four primary entities: the mobile runner client, the ASP.NET Core backend server, the PostGIS/PostgreSQL database, and external Google APIs. Live GPS coordinates recorded by the runner app are transmitted securely via API requests to the ASP.NET Core backend. The backend forwards raw route data to the Google Roads API to snap points to street networks. Once processed, spatial loop validation algorithms evaluate the route using NetTopologySuite. Validated territory polygons and workout statistics are then saved into PostGIS/PostgreSQL, which returns processed territory boundaries, updated leaderboards, and XP metrics back to the runner and spectator web views.

| Actor / User Role | Goals |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Runner** | Track real-time GPS runs, execute closed-loop routes to claim territories, manage profile stats/dashboard, earn XP/level up, and compete on individual leaderboards. |
| **Guest / Spectator** | Browse public territory maps, observe live claim feeds via the companion site, and view anonymized city-wide rankings while runner privacy/live location is protected. |
| **Clan Leader / Competition Owner** | Form and manage runner groups/clans, create and configure Zone or Distance races with custom boundaries/timeframes, and monitor clan leaderboards. |
| **Admin** | Moderate system platform activity, evaluate anti-cheat reports and flagged runs, manage user/competition approvals, and oversee overall data integrity. |

**11.1 FYP-I Features:**

1. **GPS Tracking & Territory Claiming (Core Feature):** Routes are recorded via battery-efficient background location services (using expo-location and expo-task-manager) and snapped to real-world street networks through Google Roads API. The ASP.NET Core backend leverages NetTopologySuite to confirm that the route creates an enclosed path, saving the resulting geographic boundary as claimed turf. Territory Ownership Shield & Inactivity Rule: Claimed territories remain actively shielded and protected for the owner as long as they log in or run within a 3-day activity window; competing runners traversing an active zone still earn full workout metrics (distance KM, pace, base XP), but cannot overwrite or fragment the territory. If an owner remains inactive for more than 3 consecutive days, their territory transitions to a vulnerable state, allowing other runners to conquer and claim the turf with a valid closed-loop run. Real-time runner coordinates remain strictly private.  
2. **Runner Dashboard:** Profile screens show key running routes alongside total land area controlled.  
3. **Local Leaderboards:** Players can view rankings across the city. Categories cover total territory, longest distance, territory count, and run streaks. Guests get a high-level view of city totals.  
4. **Companion Site & Guest Mode:** A Next.js website shows an interactive city territory map and a live feed of claims using Server-Sent Events. 

**11.2 FYP-II Features:**

1. **Anti-Cheat Setup:** Rejects impossible run speeds and compares  GPS   distance with phone step counts and constant speed.  
2.  **Smart Notification Engine:** Dispatches three targeted alert types: (a) Territory Shield & Status Alerts notify users via Expo Push Service when their 3-day activity shield is nearing expiration or when unshielded territories are claimed; (b) Nearby Territory Prompts trigger local prompts when entering contested zones through background geofencing; and (c) Streak Reminders deliver scheduled prompts to help maintain daily running habits.  
3. **XP & Leveling System:** XP gains scale down for repeated runs on the same route so people explore new streets. Streaks drop gradually instead of resetting instantly if you miss a day, and progress bars track badge goals clearly.  
4. **Clans with LeaderDashboards:** Users can form groups with leaders and members. PostGIS merges individual territories into combined clan maps, feeding into team leaderboards and web charts.  
5. **Two Competition Modes with Admin Dashboard:** (a) Zone Races: Organizers pick a map spot and radius (like 3 km). Only land claimed inside counts. If paths overlap, the runner with longer active session time keeps the land, or both can jump into a 15-minute distance match to decide the winner. (b) Distance Races: Runners compete for total kilometers logged during a set time frame.
